Senior Deliverability and Compliance Specialist at Kit

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2092 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realworkfromanywhere

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love.
  • Sources indicate that most Kit creators don't have a dedicated Creator Growth Manager, and when their emails start landing in spam, they need someone who can find the cause rapidly and explain it in plain language.
  • Recent findings suggest that you'll also build the playbooks, training, and AI-assisted workflows that help Support and contractors handle more deliverability questions on their own, and you'll partner with our infrastructure engineers as we run more of our sending in-house.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love. For coaches, YouTubers, authors, podcasters, and other creatives, there isn't a better marketing hub to rely on to grow audiences, automate email marketing, and sell digital products — all within one platform.More importantly, there isn't a team more committed to helping creators earn a living. We're on a mission to help creators earn $1 billion using our creator marketing platform. We have always been 100% independent and 100% remote.We are proud to have built a product that our customers love, and we look for people who have enthusiasm and belief in our mission, vision, and values to join our team. We're also embracing AI thoughtfully — both in how we build and how we hire to ensure our team is adaptable, innovative, and ready for what's next.

Sources indicate that most Kit creators don't have a dedicated Creator Growth Manager, and when their emails start landing in spam, they need someone who can find the cause rapidly and explain it in plain language. We're looking for a Deliverability and Compliance Specialist to own deliverability support for that long tail of creators, run Kit's abuse desk, and make the compliance calls that protect the sending reputation every creator on Kit shares.

Recent findings suggest that you'll also build the playbooks, training, and AI-assisted workflows that help Support and contractors handle more deliverability questions on their own, and you'll partner with our infrastructure engineers as we run more of our sending in-house. A creator can't build a lasting business if their emails don't arrive, so this work connects directly to our mission.

This is a full-time individual contributor role for someone who likes digging through headers and bounce logs to find the real cause of a problem, can explain DMARC alignment to a first-time creator without jargon, and is comfortable making a firm call when a situation is gray. You don't wait for someone to tell you what needs fixing. You proactively spot opportunities, identify patterns, and take the initiative to improve deliverability before problems arise.

You'll report to Alyssa Dulin, Director of Creator Success, and collaborate closely with:.

Our Deliverability team: a Deliverability Lead who supports our highest-value accounts and leads deliverability education, and a Deliverability Specialist who onboards and ramps up large senders moving to Kit.

Our infrastructure engineers, who run Kit's sending infrastructure.

Our compliance and anti-abuse engineers, who build the automated checks that keep spammers off Kit.

Product Specialists and the Support team, who handle the front line and escalate deliverability issues to you.

Customer Success Managers (we call them Creator Growth Managers at Kit), Sales and Migrations, and Product Managers.

According to recent reports, first Week: Get set up in Kit, our admin tools, and our support and ticketing systems, and meet our distributed team in Get To Know You chats (GTKYs). Meet the deliverability team and get an introduction on the current projects. Read our deliverability playbooks and SOPs, and get access to the monitoring tools you'll use every day: Google Postmaster Tools, Microsoft SNDS, blocklist monitoring, and our internal delivery dashboards.

Recent findings suggest that first Month: Shadow the Deliverability team and Product Specialists on deliverability tickets, account approvals, and abuse reports, then start answering queue tickets with review. Join the daily monitoring rotation (blocklist delisting, Postmaster and delivery monitoring) and the weekly Deliverability team meeting. Learn how account approvals, compliance flags, and our in-house sending platform work. By the end of the month, work deliverability tickets and abuse reports on your own and send your first delisting requests. Project: build a recurring report showing the trending deliverability ticket reasons so we understand what’s causing how to reduce friction for customers and how to solve it.

Sources indicate that first Six Months: Own the deliverability support queue for creators without a dedicated CGM: spam-folder placement, bounces, authentication and DMARC setup, and escalations from Product Specialists. Own compliance end to end, from new-account approvals and compliance flags to pausing or closing accounts that put our shared reputation at risk.Run Kit's abuse desk. You'll write and share a strategy that covers coverage, response-time targets, escalation paths, and quality checks, then put it in place so routine spam, phishing, and blocklist reports follow clear SOPs while you take the hardest cases yourself. Be the go-to contact for day-to-day mailbox provider issues with Microsoft, Gmail, Yahoo, Comcast, and regional providers, and write an incident runbook for blocklistings and provider throttling. Track the queue with a simple scorecard (volume, first response time, and escalation rate) and share what you learn with the team. Run training sessions for Support and ship your first process or AI improvements, like cleaner ticket categorization or better account data for our AI support agent, so more deliverability tickets get solved without escalation..

Recent findings suggest that first Year: Deliverability support is faster and more consistent for every creator on Kit, including the ones who never talk to a CGM. Your playbooks, help center articles, and AI-assisted workflows are what Support, CGMs, and contractors reach for first, and fewer tickets need to come to you. You've led at least one cross-team fix with infrastructure for a recurring problem you spotted in the queue, such as an alert when a creator's domain authentication breaks or a check for sudden signup spikes. You're helping shape the internal tooling and alerting our in-house sending needs, and you take part in industry groups like M3AAWG.

Deep working knowledge of email authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC, alignment, and BIMI basics), plus the ability to read raw message headers and SMTP bounce and deferral codes.

Hands-on use of Google Postmaster Tools and Microsoft SNDS/JMRP, and comfort working with major blocklists (Spamhaus, Abusix, Barracuda, Spamcop, and others) and their delisting processes.

Data fluency: you can pull bounce, complaint, and engagement data together, find the root cause, and explain it so others can act on it.

Hands-on abuse handling: you can work an abuse report or escalation start to finish, from finding the account and assessing the evidence to acting, replying to the reporter, and documenting the decision.

Process building: you can turn repeat work into SOPs, playbooks, and quality checks that a contractor or teammate can follow.

Clear, calm written communication with creators, teammates, and postmasters.

Using AI tools to research, summarize, and draft, and helping teammates do the same, with the judgment to keep a person on final compliance calls.

Experience with MTA logs or delivery observability tools (KumoMTA, PowerMTA, Postfix, Kibana/Elasticsearch, or SQL and BI tools like Mode).

Familiarity with feedback loops, spam traps, list bombing, and bot-signup patterns.

Familiarity with CAN-SPAM, CASL, and GDPR as they apply to marketing email.

Experience with Intercom, HubSpot, or a similar ticketing tool.

Experience building or tuning AI support workflows or macros.

4+ years in email deliverability, compliance, trust and safety, or technical support at an ESP, mailbox provider, or high-volume sender.

Handling escalated customer tickets end to end, including with customers who are frustrated.

Making account-level compliance or abuse decisions, such as approving, suspending, or closing accounts.

Working an abuse desk or abuse mailbox directly: spam and phishing complaints, provider and blocklist reports, and escalations.

Leading the fix for a recurring deliverability or compliance problem that needed help from more than one team.

Supporting senders on shared IP pools at an ESP.

Setting abuse or trust and safety strategy, or directing contractors or vendors on a support or abuse queue.

Working directly with mailbox provider postmaster teams.

Participating in M3AAWG or other industry groups.

Creating educational content, like help docs, training, workshops, or podcasts.

Working with creators, digital entrepreneurs, or small businesses.

You pick up problems that fall between teams without waiting for permission, and you follow them through until they're closed.

You test a hypothesis against the evidence before you act, and you frame problems clearly enough that others trust your analysis.

You protect the reputation every creator shares while staying fair and kind to the creator in front of you, and you help them understand the reasoning behind a decision.

You turn what you learn into docs, templates, and training that others use, and you adjust how you teach to fit the audience.

You hold a high bar for your work, and you push back respectfully, with data, when something puts our reputation at risk, even when Sales or leadership would prefer a different answer.

You share in-progress work and risks early so the team can solve problems together.

Treating deliverability as a set of macros rather than an investigation that needs judgment.

Discomfort saying no to a creator or a teammate when our shared reputation is at stake.

Waiting for someone to assign you work when you can already see the problem.

Needing a fixed playbook, since our sending stack and processes are changing as we bring more sending in-house.

Keeping knowledge in your head instead of writing it down for the next person.

Preferring to work without AI tools.

We're 100% remote with team members across the globe. We work mostly on East Coast time - so if you're based on the West Coast of the United States, Europe, or Asia, you might have a few early mornings or late evenings. We do our best to keep things reasonable, but a little time zone juggling comes with the territory.

For this role, we're looking for someone based in North America, with working hours that give us solid US time zone coverage of the deliverability queue.

Kit has standardized salaries based on position, no matter where you live. For this role, we're hiring at our level 3 ($118,000 USD). Level is determined based on experience and our interview process.

In a recent development, we cover up to $2,280 per month toward medical premiums, with dental and vision premiums fully covered. We offer Health Insurance looks through Aetna.

$2,000 equipment allowance for your first two years, $1,000 budget every following two years. Firm-provided laptops are issued to every Kit team member and are not included in the equipment budget.

Individual learning + development budget ($3,500/year).

Creator meetup budget ($50/month) to connect with creators over coffee, lunch, or other in-person meetups.

Childcare benefit up to $3,000 annually through JOON.

Twenty (20) days of paid time off during each year of employment.

Paid paid vacation: An after-tax bonus of $1,000 for taking five consecutive days of vacation where you’re fully unplugged from work.

Two weeks of paid sick time each year, including mental health + well being days.

Twelve (12) weeks paid parental leave and flexible scheduling in your child’s first year.

Up to six weeks of paid bereavement leave, medical leave, and disaster after six months of employment, two weeks of each paid leave in your first six months.

It has been revealed that winter Break Closure: Kit closes for a week at the end of December, giving everyone a collective break to enjoy the holiday season. Essential support services remain available, with teams coordinating to ensure coverage during this period.

Four-week, paid sabbatical after five years with the team.

Fantastic in-person or virtual retreats with the team twice a year.

We usually receive a large number of applications, and our goal is to follow up with you within two weeks. You’ll hear from us either way. Here’s what you can expect from the rest of our hiring process:.

A phone screen with our recruiter (30 min).

Hiring manager interview (45 min).

We’ll keep you informed through every step. To get started, complete this application, including a cover letter and answers to the questions on the next page. We read every single application, and your cover letter and responses help put your experience into context.

Kit is an equal opportunity employer.

In a recent development, we value diversity in all of its forms. Research tells us that applicants who are female or non-binary, as well as applicants who are people of color, are less likely to apply for roles they do not feel 100% qualified for. If you think you meet more than 50% of our requirements but fewer than 100% of them, please apply.

We’re imperfect communicators, so think of our job postings as the starting point for discussion rather than proof that you shouldn’t apply.

Kit does not discriminate on the basis of race, sex, color, religion, age, national origin, marital status, disability, veteran status, genetic information, sexual orientation, gender identity or any other reason prohibited by law in provision of employment opportunities and benefits.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love.
    • According to recent reports, our Sales team needs a dedicated data partner, and creator commerce (how creators monetize by selling digital products) is becoming a bigger part of how Kit and our creators scale.
    • It has been revealed that accurate sales data gives our team a clear picture of the pipeline and the confidence to make informed decisions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love. For coaches, YouTubers, authors, podcasters, and other creatives, there isn't a better marketing hub to rely on to grow audiences, automate email marketing, and sell digital products — all within one platform.More importantly, there isn't a team more committed to helping creators earn a living. We're on a mission to help creators earn $1 billion using our creator marketing platform. We have always been 100% independent and 100% remote.We are proud to have built a product that our customers love, and we look for people who have enthusiasm and belief in our mission, vision, and values to join our team. We're also embracing AI thoughtfully — both in how we build and how we hire to ensure our team is adaptable, innovative, and ready for what's next.

    According to recent reports, our Sales team needs a dedicated data partner, and creator commerce (how creators monetize by selling digital products) is becoming a bigger part of how Kit and our creators scale. Kit is growing, so we're looking for a Senior Analytics Engineer to own Kit's sales and commerce data from end to end.

    It has been revealed that accurate sales data gives our team a clear picture of the pipeline and the confidence to make informed decisions. That’s what makes this role so important.

    In a recent development, your primary focus will be Sales: the dbt models that turn our CRM data into trusted pipeline, deal, and funnel metrics, and the Omni dashboards our sales leader and Senior Revenue Operations Manager use to run the business. You'll also model creator commerce data, so we understand what creators sell and earn through Kit, and you'll pick up reporting work with our Product team, such as feature usage reporting. On a small data team, we step outside our usual lanes when the need is there, so the mix will shift over time.

    In a recent development, you'll build for two kinds of consumers: people and AI. Teammates increasingly answer their own questions by querying our semantic layer through Omni's AI and MCP connections to AI tools. That means your models, metric definitions, and documentation need to be clear and correct enough for an AI agent to use them without a data teammate in the loop.

    It has been revealed that this is a full-time individual contributor role for someone who likes being close to the business, enjoys turning messy operational data into numbers people trust, and is happy to work on both the models and the dashboards that sit on top of them. When Sales and Product have clear, reliable data, we help more creators build more valuable businesses with Kit.

    You'll report to Sam Umachi, Head of Data (Linkedin).

    Sales and RevOps are your primary partners, who will rely on the models and reporting you own. You'll also partner with our Product team on reporting for features like Visual Automations and on how creators use Kit.

    According to recent reports, within our data team, you'll work alongside a Staff Analytics Engineer who owns org-wide semantic layer governance and modeling standards, a Senior Data Engineer who owns ingestion and pipelines, and a Senior Business Analytics Partner focused on revenue opportunities. This role has no direct reports.

    It has been revealed that first Week: Work through our onboarding curriculum in Notion and meet the data team, our Senior Revenue Operations Manager, the sales team, and your product partners. Get set up in our core tools: dbt Cloud, GitHub, Amazon Redshift, Omni, HubSpot, Linear, Hightouch and Slack. Set up your AI-assisted development environment and learn the shared AI workflows our data team uses. Open and merge your first small pull request so you learn our review and deployment flow early.

    First Month: Map how HubSpot objects (deals, pipelines and stages, companies, contacts, and owners) flow into our dbt models, and document the gaps. Take over day-to-day ownership of the sales models and Omni dashboards that teammates have been covering. Audit current sales reporting and list where definitions differ or numbers don't reconcile. Get familiar with how commerce data (products creators sell and the revenue they earn through Kit) lands in the warehouse today. Agree with RevOps and Sales on the most crucial questions they need answered. Review teammates' pull requests and contribute to our shared SQL, dbt, and documentation standards. Share a written reflection with the team on what you've learned and where you'd focus first.

    First Six Months: Ship and maintain well-tested, documented dbt models for core sales metrics, such as pipeline, deal velocity, stage conversion, win rates, and the sales-led funnel. Expose those metrics through the Omni semantic layer, working within the team's governance standards. Rebuild or refresh the core sales dashboards so pipeline reviews and forecasting conversations run on numbers that don't need manual reconciliation. Resolve competing sales metric definitions by writing down the options and tradeoffs, aligning with Sales and RevOps, and documenting the outcome. Model creator-level commerce data, such as products sold, revenue earned through Kit, and conversion, in partnership with data engineering. Write semantic layer descriptions, metric definitions, and documentation that let Omni's AI and MCP-connected AI tools answer routine sales questions correctly, and test them against real questions from Sales, RevOps and Product. Get Sales to the point where routine questions are answered through self-serve, whether in Omni dashboards, Omni's AI, or AI tools connected over MCP, rather than one-off requests.

    First Year: Be the recognized owner of Kit's sales data, the person Sales and RevOps go to first and trust without second-guessing. Give our revenue analysis work the sales and commerce models it depends on, so deeper questions about pipeline health and creator earnings can be answered quickly, thereby enabling us to make creators more successful. Leave your domains well documented and well tested, legible to latest teammates, stakeholders, and the AI agents that query our semantic layer. Help raise the team's modeling quality through code review, pairing, and sharing what you learn.

    Industry observers note that deep dbt experience. You build modular, tested, documented dbt projects, and you're comfortable with incremental models, snapshots, macros, CI, and scheduled jobs in dbt Cloud or similar.

    In a recent development, advanced SQL. You reason carefully about grain, joins, and window functions, and you write queries that are readable and performant on a cloud warehouse.

    In a recent development, data modeling for sales and GTM. You can model deals, pipeline stages and their history, ownership changes, and funnel conversion into clean, reusable structures. You are opinionated on Kimball standards and when a concept should be a fact or dimension.

    It has been revealed that CRM data fluency. You know how sales data behaves in a CRM, including stage changes, backdated edits, and custom properties. HubSpot is preferred, but other CRM experience (e.g. Salesforce) applies just as well. We care most that you recognize common CRM patterns.

    AI-assisted development. You use AI code editors and agents (such as Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, or similar) every day, and you validate their output with tests, query results, and review before anything ships.

    Clear written communication. You explain metric definitions, tradeoffs, and data caveats in plain language that Sales, RevOps, and Product partners understand.

    BI and semantic layer experience. You can build dashboards and semantic models in Omni, Looker, or a similar BI tool, and you design metric definitions that people and AI tools can both query correctly.

    According to recent reports, git-based workflows. You keep pull requests small and well described, and you give thoughtful code review.

    Nice to have: Redshift performance tuning (sort and distribution keys), Python for scripting or API pulls, reverse ETL, and experience with product event, billing, payments, or ecommerce data.

    Around 7 or more years in analytics engineering or data engineering where you personally shipped production data models.

    Several years of hands-on work building and maintaining production dbt projects.

    Working directly with sales teams and RevOps, and owning reporting they relied on to run the business.

    Owning a data domain over time and evolving its models as the business and its questions changed.

    Working at a SaaS manufacturer, ideally one with both a self-serve and a sales-led motion. Commerce, payments, or creator economy experience is a plus, not a requirement.

    Working on a small or remote team where you were trusted to make decisions independently.

    Ownership and follow-through. You treat your data domains as yours. You notice problems before stakeholders do, close the loop on requests, and finish what you start.

    Judgment. You match rigor to the decision at hand, know when a quick answer is enough and when a request should become a durable model, and say so clearly.

    Recent findings suggest that flexibility. You're glad to step outside your primary area when another team needs help, and you balance that work against your core commitments openly.

    Sources indicate that teach everything you know. You document as you go, pair generously, and help stakeholders understand the data well enough to use it on their own.

    Work in public. You share progress, open questions, and decisions in writing where the team can see them, including what didn't work.

    Industry observers note that creator success is our success. You remember who's on the other end. A wrong number in a pipeline review means Sales spends time on the wrong creators, and that shapes how carefully you work.

    Recent findings suggest that do it with excellence. You test your work, review it carefully, and don't ship a number you can't defend.

    Candor with care. You're comfortable pushing back when a request won't answer the real question, and you do it in a way that builds trust.

    Needing detailed specs or a highly structured environment before you can start.

    Recent findings suggest that discomfort with ambiguity. Some of our sales and commerce definitions are still evolving, and you'll help settle them.

    Needing several layers of approval to make modeling decisions within your domain.

    Wanting to work only on dashboards, or only on pipelines, rather than across the transformation and BI layers.

    In a recent development, wanting a strictly fixed scope. Sales comes first, but you'll pick up Product or other work when the business needs it.

    Recent findings suggest that wanting mostly greenfield work. Much of this role is improving sales models and dashboards that already exist.

    Preferring to take tickets as written rather than partnering with stakeholders on what they need.

    Being skeptical of AI's capabilities, or using AI without good judgment and accountability.

    Expecting a large data team with dedicated specialists for every part of the stack.

    We're 100% remote with team members across the globe. We work mostly on East Coast time - so if you're based on the West Coast of the United States, Europe, or Asia, you might have a few early mornings or late evenings. We do our best to keep things reasonable, but a little time zone juggling comes with the territory.

    In a recent development, kit has standardized salaries based on position, no matter where you live. For this role, we're hiring at our level 4 ($172,000). Level is determined based on experience and our interview process.

    We cover up to $2,280 per month toward medical premiums, with dental and vision premiums fully covered. We offer Health Insurance plans through Aetna.

    $2,000 equipment allowance for your first two years, $1,000 budget every following two years. Firm-provided laptops are issued to every Kit team member and are not included in the equipment budget.

    Individual learning + development budget ($3,500/year).

    Creator meetup budget ($50/month) to connect with creators over coffee, lunch, or other in-person meetups.

    Childcare benefit up to $3,000 annually through JOON.

    Twenty (20) days of paid time off during each year of employment.

    Paid paid vacation: An after-tax bonus of $1,000 for taking five consecutive days of vacation where you’re fully unplugged from work.

    Two weeks of paid sick time each year, including mental health + well being days.

    Twelve (12) weeks paid parental leave and flexible scheduling in your child’s first year.

    Up to six weeks of paid bereavement leave, medical leave, and disaster after six months of employment, two weeks of each paid leave in your first six months.

    It has been revealed that winter Break Closure: Kit closes for a week at the end of December, giving everyone a collective break to enjoy the holiday season. Essential support services remain available, with teams coordinating to ensure coverage during this period.

    Four-week, paid sabbatical after five years with the team.

    Fantastic in-person or virtual retreats with the team twice a year.

    We usually receive a large number of applications, and our goal is to follow up with you within two weeks. You’ll hear from us either way. Here’s what you can expect from the rest of our hiring process:.

    A phone screen with our recruiter (30 min).

    Hiring manager interview (45 min).

    Recent findings suggest that we’ll keep you informed through every step. To get started, complete this application, including a cover letter and answers to the questions on the next page. We read every single application, and your cover letter and responses help put your experience into context.

    Kit is an equal opportunity employer.

    We value diversity in all of its forms. Research tells us that applicants who are female or non-binary, as well as applicants who are people of color, are less likely to apply for roles they do not feel 100% qualified for. If you think you meet more than 50% of our requirements but fewer than 100% of them, please apply.

    We’re imperfect communicators, so think of our job postings as the starting point for discussion rather than proof that you shouldn’t apply.

    Kit does not discriminate on the basis of race, sex, color, religion, age, national origin, marital status, disability, veteran status, genetic information, sexual orientation, gender identity or any other reason prohibited by law in provision of employment opportunities and benefits.

    Latest Update: How Elex Michaelson Fills CNN’s West Coast Gap

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Elex Michaelson got a firsthand look at CNN journalists working a breaking news situation during the White House Correspondents’ Dinner in April.
    • Michaelson was one of the network’s guests that evening at the Washington Hilton, in Washington, D.C.
    • “The shooting itself was a very strange experience, and to see everybody get to work in their tuxes and trying to figure out what happened was also something I’ll never forget,” stated Michaelson.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Elex Michaelson got a firsthand look at CNN journalists working a breaking news situation during the White House Correspondents’ Dinner in April.

    Michaelson was one of the network’s guests that evening at the Washington Hilton, in Washington, D.C. He described being there as a “wonderful experience,” but it took a sharp turn when shots rang out within the building, and the president was promptly evacuated.

    “The shooting itself was a very strange experience, and to see everybody get to work in their tuxes and trying to figure out what happened was also something I’ll never forget,” stated Michaelson.

    The Los Angeles-based anchor of CNN’s late-night program, The Story Is, airing from 12 to 2 a.m. ET, Michaelson is no stranger to handling breaking news situations. He broke two major international news stories this year: he was the first to report when the US undertook military strikes and captured Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela in January, and he was also the first to report on the Iran bombings in March, both of which, coincidentally, happened around the same time on a Friday night at around 10:30 p.m. PT/1:30 a.m. ET. This past Friday, he was on the air for four hours as part of CNN’s continuous coverage of the FAA issuing a ground stop for all the planes across the entire country.

    Speaking to TVNewser, Michaelson noted, “CNN does a lot of things well, but I think it does breaking news best of all.”.

    For the Venezuelan military strikes, Michaelson recalls how they were covering a pop culture story when a producer told him over his earpiece that there were explosions in Caracas. In that moment, he realized who he was working for.

    “We stated goodbye to the people, to a quick commercial break reset, and then we were off, and it was a reminder of just the global power of CNN.”.

    It has been revealed that michaelson joined CNN in September 2025, bringing his West Coast sensibilities to the network. Before that, he was an anchor for the LA-based Fox affiliate KTTV 11 and earlier worked as a reporter at KABC-TV in Los Angeles and as a weekend morning anchor and weeknight reporter for XETV in San Diego (when the Tijuana-based station had English-language operations and a news department there). This past October, he and his team celebrated the first anniversary of The Story Is, which he describes as serving a niche that didn’t exist before: an audience in the western part of the U.S. that didn’t have a live news program airing during primetime hours in that region.

    “I think we’ve filled that gap,” he mentioned. Adding, “I think we’ve also brought some fresh voices that you don’t see on cable news all day long that have a lot to say and are a valuable addition to the conversation.”.

    Recent findings suggest that in its first year, according to CNN, The Story Is with Elex Michaelson has seen its total viewer audience grow by 15% since launch, compared with the six-month pre-launch period. It also led cable news among adults 25–54 when news broke of U.S. strikes on Venezuela on January 2, 2026 (1:45 – 2 a.m. ET). The show now attracts nearly one in four viewers in the Adults 25–54 demo in its Pacific time slot, up from one in five before launch, and is No. 1 in cable news among Hispanic viewers in its time slot, both in total viewers and the demo.

    It has been revealed that the Story Is goes beyond politics, covering the news with a West Coast, laid-back feel. Michaelson said CNN president Mark Thompson described the program as “the most upbeat show on CNN,” and the anchor pointed out that during those hours they have had thoughtful entertainment conversations, profiled athletes involved in their communities, and shared other community service stories.

    “I love politics, but I also am particularly proud of some of these profile stories that we’ve done with celebrities,” Michaelson mentioned. “I really love the sit-down we did with William Shatner and his daughter, both of whom had just battled stage four cancer and survived it.”.

    Recent findings suggest that he touted the advantage of anchoring out of CNN’s LA bureau, which lets him showcase those types of stories. “If I was in Washington, you’re competing with like a thousand other reporters doing the same thing, on Capitol Hill, for example, but in this space there is more room to do something unique, which has been fun.”.

    It has been revealed that as for the show’s first anniversary, amid the busy news cycle, Michaelson brought in pizza and toasted with champagne after the show to mark the occasion. He hopes to have a proper celebration in the near future now that the midterm elections have concluded.

    It has been revealed that mark Mwachiro is a TVNewser contributor who has been writing for the blog since March 2022. Based out of New York, Mark has also contributed to ADWEEK.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, 16% — Walt Disney Co.
    • $3 billion — Total annual cost-cutting savings run rate Disney expect by fiscal 2029 through layoffs, procurement and other efficiencies.
    • 24% — Increase in aggregated viewership of Monday Night Football through the first nine weeks of the NFL season, a good sign heading into Disney’s first-ever Super Bowl broadcast.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, 16% — Walt Disney Co. revenue growth for the fiscal fourth quarter ended Oct. 3, inflated more than 7 percentage points by a 53rd week in the current fiscal year. Earnings per share also grew 16%, even adjusting out that 53rd week effect.

    $3 billion — Total annual cost-cutting savings run rate Disney expect by fiscal 2029 through layoffs, procurement and other efficiencies.

    24% — Increase in aggregated viewership of Monday Night Football through the first nine weeks of the NFL season, a good sign heading into Disney’s first-ever Super Bowl broadcast.

    For a company anticipating significant layoffs over the next two years, there was a lot of good news.

    The September Ohio State-Texas college football broadcast on ESPN drew 14 million viewers, ESPN’s biggest audience for a college game in 10 years, per Disney’s shareholder letter. U.S. Open viewership came in at four-year highs.

    Disney CEO Josh D’Amaro expects more major things from the Marvel Comics Universe with Avengers Doomsday opening next month, building on the theatrical momentum of summer’s Spider-Man: Brand Fresh Day and the best month ever for MCU viewership on Disney+ in August, he said on the company’s earnings call.

    Disney+ also tapped a South Korean creative pipeline once dominated by Netflix with The Remarried Empress, which on Nov. 3 had the biggest premiere ever for a local original across Disney+ and Hulu globally, D’Amaro said: “We haven’t even begun to see the benefits of our investment in international content.”.

    Next month, Disney+ will begin incorporating TikTok creator content as part of its agreement with that platform, D’Amaro noted, adding that the manufacturer is continuing to explore the option of a Disney+ free tier “to reach a more price-sensitive consumer.”.

    According to recent reports, expansion of the NCAA College Football Playoff to 24 teams, and from 11 to 23 games next year, promises an even bigger sports rights earnings take for Disney. “ESPN is going to have exclusive rights to all the rounds,” D’Amaro stated. “We’ve got broad distribution flexibility across ABC and ESPN.”.

    The CEO declined to disclose the rights costs, and acknowledged that Disney has sub-licensing rights, but didn’t commit to any plans to get outside networks involved.

    “Changes like these are not easy, and they affect people who care deeply about Disney and have contributed so much to this firm. At the same time, these steps are important if we want to be a company that moves faster, adapts to a rapidly changing environment, and keeps investing in the content and technology that will drive our growth. We make these choices because we believe so strongly in what Disney can be.” —Disney CEO Josh D’Amaro on impending layoffs.

    Jack Neff is interim TV, Sports and Media Editor at ADWEEK. He is formerly editor at large for Ad Age and has covered media, measurement, household, and personal care marketing, as well as Walmart and other areas. He’s formerly written for The Atlanta Journal-Constitution, Bloomberg, and a variety of trade publications, as well as authoring business books for woodworkers, graphic designers, and freelance writers.

    A Crash Course in Marketing to Machines

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1524 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adweek

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Some years ago, one of us, Jim Lecinski, wrote a manifesto called the “Zero Moment of Truth,” or “ZMOT,” which argued that before the traditional point of purchase arrives — before a customer reaches the shampoo aisle shelf or the car dealer’s lot -— that customer goes looking for evidence to help them decide what products are the most credible and therefore what to buy.
    • Recent findings suggest that many marketers still begin the marketing process from the organization out: Who are we?
    • They begin by asking what job the customer is trying to get done, how that customer moves through the purchase journey, what questions arise along the way, and which sources shape confidence and choice.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Some years ago, one of us, Jim Lecinski, wrote a manifesto called the “Zero Moment of Truth,” or “ZMOT,” which argued that before the traditional point of purchase arrives — before a customer reaches the shampoo aisle shelf or the car dealer’s lot -— that customer goes looking for evidence to help them decide what products are the most credible and therefore what to buy.

    Recent findings suggest that many marketers still begin the marketing process from the organization out: Who are we? What do we want to sell? What message can we create to persuade people to buy? In effect, they are working their way from the product to the customer. Great marketers, however, work the other way around.

    They begin by asking what job the customer is trying to get done, how that customer moves through the purchase journey, what questions arise along the way, and which sources shape confidence and choice. Then they align their go-to-market accordingly.

    Industry observers note that digital marketing has made the customer decision process more complex. Rather than relying on a single message or source, customers consult multiple sources before deciding what to buy. They gather evidence. They search, compare, read what other customers say, watch experts and creators, and increasingly ask AI assistants for answers and recommendations.

    In a recent development, the original three sources – search engines, social conversations, and ratings and reviews – remain important. But two others now deserve a place in the ZMOT framework: content creators and AI assistants. Both influence how customers evaluate choices, form preferences, and make purchase decisions.

    Industry observers note that and these sources also interact. Search results show online community discussions, reviews, and creator videos. Creator content influences people and AI-generated answers. AI assistants draw from information created across the web, synthesize it, and increasingly build or narrow the consideration set on the customer’s behalf.

    The Zero Moment of Truth provides the clearest framework for understanding this change.

    The concept of the Zero Moment remains as relevant today as when it was introduced: The Zero Moment of Truth is the critical pre-purchase period when customers seek information, compare options, reduce uncertainty, and form preferences. A stimulus creates awareness or activates a need. Before the traditional point of purchase arrives, the customer goes looking for evidence that will help them decide what to believe and what to choose.

    What continues to evolve are the sources customers use to gather the information that shapes this decision-making zero moment.

    Sources indicate that content Creators help customers understand categories, interpret differences, see products in context, and decide with confidence. AI assistants increasingly answer questions, compare alternatives, form shortlists, analyze options, and recommend specific brands.

    In a recent development, the expansion of avenues from which customers acquire knowledge, requires marketers to rethink their approach. A customer considering a new suitcase may move among search, online community discussions, ratings & reviews, content creator videos, and an AI chatbot all during a single decision journey. These five sources therefore form an interconnected portfolio rather than separate or sequential channels.

    It has been revealed that therefore, winning the Zero Moment still requires clear and persuasive brand messages across these various avenues. The marketer’s mandate now extends beyond the messages the brand creates and distributes. The expanded Zero Moment requires marketers to move from managing brand messages alone to managing the broader body of decision evidence that customers and AI systems use to understand, evaluate, and choose brands. Each source has a distinct role:.

    It has been revealed that these roles overlap, which is precisely why marketers must manage them together. Creator videos appear in search results. Online community conversations influence both human perceptions and AI-generated answers. Reviews shape search visibility, customer trust, and machine-generated comparisons. Brand content can support every source when it is useful, clear, current, and corroborated by evidence outside the brand.

    It has been revealed that notice that AI assistants differ from the other four sources because they play two roles. They are a fifth source customers consult directly, and they synthesize information drawn from the other four. This becomes even more important as AI is directly embedded across categories, including social, ecommerce and productivity.

    Sources indicate that an AI-generated answer may incorporate search results, brand websites, publishers, social conversations, reviews, creator content, and other third-party evidence. AI increasingly assembles and interprets the consideration set on the customer’s behalf. It can identify contradictions, surface recurring criticisms, compare claims, and omit brands that lack sufficient credible evidence from the answers or recommendations it provides. In fact, Google recently introduced newly introduced ad formats including Conversational Discovery Ads, Direct Offers, and Highlighted Ads, which answer questions, supply analysis and offer suggestions right inside the ad creative.

    Strong search rankings no longer guarantee visibility in AI-generated answers. A brand may perform well in search engines but be missing from the recommendations from AI assistants or overviews. It may have a polished website while customers, creators, and reviewers tell a different story elsewhere. It may appear across all five sources with inconsistent product information, claims, pricing, or positioning.

    Each source can strengthen or weaken the evidence found in the others.

    Marketers still need persuasive messages, which are an essential part of the evidence customers encounter.

    Marketers have traditionally focused on the messages they create and distribute. Today, they also must understand and influence the evidence customers encounter elsewhere, including reviews and creator content and AI-generated recommendations.

    Decision evidence is the accumulated body of information, experiences, claims, reviews, demonstrations, conversations, and third-party validation that shapes what customers and AI systems understand and believe about a brand.

    This evidence includes useful and authoritative brand content, accurate product information, strong customer experiences, current ratings and reviews, credible third-party coverage, informed creator content, and consistent facts that both humans and machines can understand. YouTube becomes a valuable source of authority, based on the way large language models prioritize multimodal content and direct video citations. A recent BrightEdge report indicates that a brand’s YouTube presence represents a unique path to AI optimization. As the dominant video platform in AI search, YouTube is already capturing nearly 30% of AI citations in Google’s AI Overviews (source).

    In a recent development, while brands cannot fully control every source they can influence the quality, availability, credibility, and coherence of the evidence customers encounter. The goal is to ensure that the evidence available across all five sources supports the position the brand wants to earn in the customer’s mind.

    To help marketers see how effectively their brand appears during the Zero Moment of Truth we’ve developed a helpful Zero Moment Five-Source Evidence Check.

    According to recent reports, start with the three to five questions that matter most in the customer’s decision. These might include:.

    Then examine what a customer would find about the brand across search engines, social conversations, ratings and reviews, content creators, and AI assistants. For each source, assess five things:.

    Record your brand’s results for each source as Strong, Weak, or Absent (See Fig 2). The weak and absent cells reveal the most key evidence gaps.

    With the completed diagnostic in hand, the next step is to close the gaps. Prioritize the weak or absent areas most likely to influence customer choice, assign clear owners and actions, and strengthen the underlying evidence through better content, corrected information, stronger customer experiences, review management, creator engagement, or credible third-party validation.

    Then repeat the check regularly. The goal is to move every priority area toward Strong and keep it there as customer behavior, platform results, and AI-generated answers continue to change.

    The expanded Zero Moment requires marketers to move from managing brand messages alone to managing the decision evidence customers and AI systems use to understand, evaluate, and choose brands.

    The challenge for marketers is no longer about getting the right message in front of the right customer. It’s ensuring that when customers – or AI agents – look for evidence, they find information that is accurate and credible while also maintaining a consistent brand promise.

    In a recent development, jim Lecinski is a Clinical Professor of Marketing at Northwestern University's Kellogg School of Management where he has won multiple prestigious teaching awards including Kellogg Professor of the Year. His career includes twelve years at Google, where he was vp of customer solutions for the Americas. Lecinski's seminal book “Winning the Zero Moment of Truth” has been read by over 300,000 marketers, and his latest project, “The AI Marketing Canvas: A Five Step AI Initiative for Marketers” has been named both a top AI book and a top business book.

    Kelly Cutler brings together industry experience and academic expertise in her role as Clinical Associate Professor at Northwestern University, where she teaches marketing and communication across multiple schools and programs. She also serves as Associate Director of Research at the Spiegel Research Center, focusing on AI integration and the evolving digital marketing landscape. Kelly is regularly featured in both academic and industry publications and speaks at conferences and events around the world. She remains actively engaged with industry, advising organizations and delivering executive education and professional development programs to global audiences.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    According to recent reports, we're hiring a Product Manager to own Postgres itself at Supabase. Every Supabase project is a full Postgres database, and Postgres is the foundation that Auth, Storage, Realtime and Edge Functions run on. You'll own the product experience of the database: Postgres versions and upgrades, maintenance, observability, extensions and security.

    Industry observers note that you'll work closely with our Postgres engineering teams and with the PM lead for Databases, who leads Multigres. You'll define the Postgres requirements that architecture must meet, and own how customers experience their database through that transition.

    According to recent reports, this role is ideal for someone who loves Postgres, sweats the details that make a database trustworthy, and is excited about improving the experience for millions of developers. Small improvements here compound across every project on the platform.

    Sources indicate that you'll own Postgres versions, upgrades and end-of-life. Which major and minor versions we support, how and when customers upgrade, and how we retire old versions. Your goal is to make upgrades routine rather than risky.

    In a recent development, you'll make maintenance predictable. You'll design how we schedule, communicate and run maintenance windows so customers stay informed and in control, and disruption is rare and expected.

    You'll help developers understand their database. Query performance, metrics, logs and advisors: you'll own the path from "my database is slow" to the fix.

    You'll own our extension ecosystem. Which extensions we offer, how we evaluate and support new ones, and how we keep them working across versions.

    You'll own Postgres security. Roles and permissions, Row Level Security ergonomics, secure defaults, and how we respond to Postgres and extension CVEs.

    You'll talk to developers across the full spectrum, from indie developers on their first project to enterprises running critical workloads, and bring what you learn into every prioritization call.

    You'll own the problem definition, requirements and success metrics for what we ship, such as upgrade success rate, the share of the fleet on supported versions, and time-to-diagnose for performance problems. You'll set the metric before the team builds, then track it after launch.

    You'll keep Engineering, Support and GTM aligned. You'll own the plan of record for what's coming, why, and in what order, and communicate version changes and deprecations clearly to customers.

    Recent findings suggest that 4+ years of Product Management experience on databases, developer tools or infrastructure, or equivalent depth as an engineer, DBA or founder moving into product. You're comfortable commenting on an architecture doc and advocating for the user when trade-offs are required.

    Know Postgres well, or another relational database well enough to ramp quickly. You're comfortable reading EXPLAIN output and talking about replication, WAL, roles and extensions.

    Have shipped products where reliability and trust are the experience. You treat downtime and breaking changes as product problems, not just operational ones.

    Sources indicate that write clearly. Your specs, announcements and deprecation notices leave little room for confusion.

    Recent findings suggest that build with what you own. You run queries, test upgrades and try extensions yourself, and form opinions through first-hand use.

    It has been revealed that use AI to move faster. You use AI tools to compress research, drafting and feedback synthesis so you spend more time on judgment calls.

    Work async by default. Supabase is fully remote. You make decisions in writing and move work forward without meetings.

    Worked on a managed database service.

    Ran Postgres in production: upgrades, tuning, incident response.

    Worked on database observability, performance tooling, or security and compliance products.

    Contributed to Postgres, its extensions, or the wider open-source community.

    Shipped something using Supabase.

    Industry observers note that we hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Industry observers note that every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are crucial to us.

    Once a year, the entire organization gathers in a newly introduced city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    In a recent development, we operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    Industry observers note that we move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Editor’s note: Brave Bison, which acquired Mark Ritson’s MiniMBA in 2025, owns about 28% of System1 and sought to acquire the rest this year.
    • Joy is stuck at the airport on Christmas Eve, the snow coming down hard, and every flight cancelled.
    • Recent findings suggest that this is “Joy Delivered”, Amazon’s new holiday ad, which debuted earlier this month and runs like a proper movie.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Editor’s note: Brave Bison, which acquired Mark Ritson’s MiniMBA in 2025, owns about 28% of System1 and sought to acquire the rest this year.

    Joy is stuck at the airport on Christmas Eve, the snow coming down hard, and every flight cancelled. So she picks up her bag of presents and sets off for home the long way: a bus, a lift from some donkey farmers, a night in a boat cabin on a heaving sea, a taxi driven by a giant. At every stop, she thanks a stranger with one of the Amazon parcels meant for her family.

    Recent findings suggest that this is “Joy Delivered”, Amazon’s new holiday ad, which debuted earlier this month and runs like a proper movie. A new version of the Beatles’ “Golden Slumbers” does a lot of the emotional heavy lifting and the hug at the end will get you.

    There are two problems with the ad, however. One is peripheral. One central.

    In a recent development, the peripheral one first. Amazon filmed its white Christmas in Latest Zealand, in and around Dunedin, to be specific. But it’s summer down there, and it will be even warmer by Christmas, when most of the country will be at the beach in a pair of shorts.

    According to recent reports, the central problem is bigger. Amazon already has a great Christmas ad: “Joy Ride.”.

    Industry observers note that three old ladies sitting on a snowy hill watch the local kids go sledding. One of them orders some seat cushions from Amazon. The box turns up and the next thing you know they are flying down the hill and, for a few seconds, they are girls again. There are no words. Just an instrumental of “In My Life.”.

    “Joy Ride” first ran in 2023 and got the maximum 5.8 stars from System1. Basically perfection.

    Then Amazon did something very unusual for a massive marketer. Last year, instead of making a newly introduced ad, it ran the old one again. It scored 5.7, again putting it in the rare tech giant of less than 1% of all ads made all year.

    According to recent reports, none of this should surprise anyone. Coca-Cola first ran “Holidays Are Coming” in 1995. The trucks have rolled out every Christmas since, and System1 notes the ad always scores five stars in its testing. When System1 looked at more than 50,000 ads, it found that scores barely move as ads get older, and that some of the very best actually improve as people get to know them.

    Ads don’t wear out, at least not for consumers.

    It has been revealed that amazon’s problem is that its advertising decisions are made by marketers — people who like to make new, shiny stuff. Jo Shoesmith, Amazon’s global chief brand officer, told ADWEEK that people want nostalgia but also “something they haven’t seen before.”.

    I call that a complete contradiction.

    In a recent development, the average brand building campaign reaches its maximum impact about two to three years into execution. Seasonal stuff can often, as Coke has proved, live on for decades. But the average marketer is tired of their ad, and wants to make something newly introduced.

    In a recent development, it’s the same story with slogans, with logos, with distinctive brand assets. Marketers forget they are not the consumer. They look at their ads for at least 9,000 hours before they release it into the wild, and are over it before most of the target market has noticed it.

    There is an intermediate position. Amazon could pull a Coca-Cola: bring out their old ad every year but also make a crappy, inferior new execution alongside it. But why create a bat to beat yourself with? Better to remove the outstanding, already made, already free, already proven, already much-loved Christmas ad completely, and then run something less good, with lots more risk and cost attached. Makes perfect sense.

    We read all the time that marketers need more support from their CEO, more budget, more seats in the boardroom.

    Industry observers note that but what they mostly need is patience. It takes years, not months, for a good campaign to work. Amazon knew that last Christmas, but it has already forgotten it.

    Sources indicate that mark Ritson has a PhD in Marketing and spent 25 years working as a marketing professor, and has also worked as both a global brand consultant and as the in-house brand consultant for LVMH. His articles have appeared in the Sloan Management Review, Harvard Business Review, the Journal of Advertising and the Journal of Consumer Research.

    Recent findings suggest that product Building is how Camunda's Experience organization builds the applications people use on top of Camunda 8, such as Hub, Operate, and ProcessOS.     The IDP & RPA pod builds how Camunda processes work with documents and legacy applications. With intelligent document processing (IDP), customers create extraction and classification templates in Camunda Hub and publish them so a process can use AI to turn invoices and other documents into structured data. With robotic process automation (RPA), customers integrate legacy applications that have no APIs, using Robot Framework scripts on a standalone RPA worker.     In a recent development, supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    According to recent reports, we're looking for a Head of Ecosystem to lead the teams that make Supabase the backend for the platforms and tools developers already use. You'll build this org from the ground up and shape how Supabase extends beyond its own platform.

    You'll also drive hiring, onboarding, and career development while maintaining high engineering standards.

    Build and lead a latest engineering org across platform partners, integrations, and Marketplace, hiring EMs and engineers as it grows.

    Own the technical relationship with the platforms building on Supabase, from integration health to escalations.

    Set and maintain clear roadmaps that balance partner needs with platform priorities.

    Maintain high engineering standards: roadmap hygiene, issue tracking, on-call, incident response, and responsiveness to partners.

    Proven experience leading multiple engineering teams, including managing other managers.

    Experience building and running platform, API, or integration surfaces that third parties depend on in production.

    Technical credibility with partner engineering teams, and the judgment to say no.

    Experience building teams or an org from a small base, including hiring and developing engineering managers.

    Experience managing remote, globally distributed teams.

    • Some of the people who have witnessed all these changes up close are the executive producers of MS NOW’s linear shows.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that on November 15, 2025, Versant switched the name of its news network from MSNBC to MS NOW. The new name, which stands for My Source for News, Opinion and the World, had to build alot of its infrastructure from scratch after detaching from NBC News.

    Recent findings suggest that the switch to a fresh name did not affect viewership, as the network ranked second among all cable networks in total viewers during the third quarter. In addition, in the past year it launched its direct-to-consumer platform, MS NOW Membership.

    Some of the people who have witnessed all these changes up close are the executive producers of MS NOW’s linear shows. They have been responsible for establishing the new name in their programs as well as ensuring the mission remains the same even after the transition.

    Sources indicate that in recognition of MS NOW’s first anniversary, TVNewser spoke to five executive producers, who released new shows within the first year. They Include, State of Play with Peter Alexander’s Sandi Cohen, On the Line with Alicia Menendez’s Marti Hause, The 11th Hour with Ali Velshi’s Rebekah Dryden, Connect with Jacob Soboroff’s Dina Moss, and Joy Fowlin from The Assignment with Antonia Hylton.

    (This interview has been edited for length).

    TVNewser: How has the first year known as MS NOW been?

    Cohen: I’ve only been here for the last six months, but the energy is unmatched. There’s a feeling of positivity and building towards the future, and a real team effort to do so. It’s been inspiring and given me a boost.

    In a recent development, hause: It has been a really exciting year at MS NOW. It’s been remarkable to see this entire organization build from the ground up, driving toward the ultimate goal of serving our viewers.

    Dryden: I think of the first year as MS NOW as a year of proving it, a series of rapid-fire, real-time proof points of who we are and what we can do as a network, standing up on our own.

    Recent findings suggest that moss: When MS NOW first relaunched, I never would have imagined we’d be here. It’s been the greatest honor and challenge to launch Connect alongside Jacob and our team.

    It has been revealed that fowlin: Two words to describe the first year as MS NOW: seamless and exciting. Change can be hard, but everyone worked together to make the transition as smooth as possible. It was truly a testament of leading from the top.

    TN: What does the upcoming network name signify for you and your program?

    Recent findings suggest that cohen: We’re meeting the moment! “NOW” is right in the name. A constant reminder of why we do what we do, and to meet that mission.

    Hause: The latest name signifies to me that we are covering the day’s news with hosts, reporters and guests who bring a depth of expertise and experience to help our viewers navigate the stakes of what we are seeing.

    Dryden: “News, Opinion, World” has always been our work. But I especially love what “My Source” says about who we’ve become. By 11 o’clock, people have had the whole day’s news thrown at them. Being someone’s source means answering that with facts they can trust, and then sending them to bed with something to hold onto.

    It has been revealed that moss: We hope that our audience sees us as their ‘source’ for connection and community. What we’ve really been prioritizing on Connect are voices and stories that our viewers can relate to.

    Fowlin: MS NOW stands for accuracy, precision, and collaboration. I am so proud to work with a team and an entire network of people who truly enjoy coming to work every day.

    TN: As the leaders of new programs on MS NOW, how has it gone so far?

    Cohen: We’re having a blast. Nearly every day Peter tells me how fun doing this show is. And he’s right. We have a wonderful team of smart and kind producers who work incredibly hard.

    Hause: It has been such an invigorating process. Starting a new show has been a total reset on how we cover the news of the day. For On The Line, it’s a constant discussion about how we focus on the stakes of any given story, not the odds. Dryden: It has been a joy to lead a new chapter of The 11th Hour with Ali Velshi. We both feel so privileged to have been given the opportunity to take up the 11th Hour mantle and trusted with the freedom to make it our own.

    According to recent reports, moss: Long nights, early mornings, and a ton of coffee! But the most fun I’ve had in my career.

    Fowlin: Launching The Assignment has been one of the best opportunities of my career. I had never built a show from scratch, and what a privilege it was to do. I inherited an incredible team of producers who embraced the show’s vision.

    TN: What similarities have you seen between relaunching MS NOW and starting a fresh program?

    Cohen: Our show has had to find our voice, our people, and our mission. It takes a lot of trial and error. Leaders across the tech giant are doing the same thing. Whether that’s for our digital products, in-person experiences, or linear TV.

    It has been revealed that hause: I see a lot of similarities in the way we’ve questioned conventional wisdom and our processes. It’s led to some great changes to the status quo and brought newly introduced opportunities for members of our team.

    It has been revealed that dryden: Cable news producers have always been a scrappy and industrious group, and there was a real sense of building something together as we introduced this new show and this new network. So every challenge felt like a team effort and, in the end, an accomplishment.

    According to recent reports, moss: What I’ve enjoyed so much is the collaboration. When we relaunched MS NOW, there was collective effort to make it a success. I feel the same about launching Connect with Jacob Soboroff. It’s been a melding of minds (and some of the brightest minds in the industry, at that).

    Fowlin: Yes, putting together a fresh show does require a start-up mentality. You need grit, drive, flexibility, and a good dose of fearlessness. We all come together with the same mission: to put together a news program centered on the human stories behind the headlines.

    TN: What’s one interesting nugget you can share about your anchor?

    Industry observers note that cohen: Peter Alexander does not drink coffee. Even when we’re traveling and working long days, there is no caffeine, and he really doesn’t need it.

    Hause: She just planned her 8th-grade class reunion.

    According to recent reports, dryden: I think Ali has a reputation for being very serious. But behind the scenes, he doesn’t take himself seriously – he’s just really funny and warm..

    Moss: Jacob will respond to viewers on social media during commercial breaks. And sometimes, if you tell him to slip a random word into the newscast…he just might do it.

    Fowlin: Antonia is an incredibly hard-working anchor and reporter. And she’s also a dedicated Real Housewives fan. When we’re not talking about story ideas or guest requests, we’re texting about whatever wild and crazy thing happened on the latest episode.

    According to recent reports, hi there! We're hiring an Information Security Engineer with a focus on Application Security to join our Information Security team at Camunda.

    We are a team that takes security seriously without making it feel like a locked door. We work in a transparent, straightforward way, and we care about doing the work right rather than just checking a compliance box.

    Sources indicate that you will work side by side with our R&D engineers: reviewing designs, threat modeling fresh features, digging into code and helping teams make good, risk-based decisions about the vulnerabilities that come in. You'll also help build the internal tools that make this work scale, including our CVE registry and the LLM-assisted workflows we use to analyse code and triage findings.

    Camunda is an AI-first company, and InfoSec is no exception: AI agents are part of how we review code, assess vulnerabilities, and build our tools. You will help shape how that works.

    According to recent reports, this is a hands-on role for someone who already has solid AppSec foundations and wants to grow. We are a generalist team, so you will also take part in our on-call rotation and incident response, and get exposure to other areas of security. But most of your time will be spent with engineers and building and maintaining internal tools and processes.

    Vulnerability management: triage findings from SCA, container and code scanning, external reports and internal security testing; assess whether Camunda is actually affected; agree fix / mitigate / accept with engineering and follow through to release.

    Threat modeling and security reviews: run threat modeling sessions and design reviews with R&D teams for newly introduced features and architecture changes, and turn the results into concrete, prioritised actions.

    Code analysis with LLMs: use and improve LLM-assisted tooling (agents, prompts, reusable skills) to review code, validate findings and reproduce challenges, while applying your own judgement to know when the model is wrong.

    Build internal security tooling: contribute to the CVE registry and related automation that connects scanners, engineering teams, and customer communication. Much of it is built on Camunda itself.

    Help engineers do the secure thing by default: answer questions, review pull requests, improve guidelines and occasionally run a session or workshop.

    On-call and incident response: share the InfoSec on-call rotation with the other engineers and help investigate and resolve security incidents.

    Support the wider team: help write security advisories for our customers, answer customer security questions and support audits.

    What You Will Bring to the Role.

    Around 3+ years in security or software engineering, with at least 2 of them working on application or product security (AppSec, product security, pentesting, or a security-focused developer role all count).

    Experience at a SaaS or software product organization, working closely with engineering teams that ship often through modern CI/CD and cloud environments.

    Hands-on vulnerability triage: you've worked with tools like Snyk, Trivy, Semgrep, CodeQL or similar, can tell a real issue from a false positive, and can explain how exploitable something actually is in context (CVSS, exploitability, configuration).

    In a recent development, threat modeling and design review experience (e.g. STRIDE) on real systems, ideally web apps, APIs, or distributed services.

    You read and write code. You're comfortable reading Java (Camunda is built on it) well enough to follow a data flow and spot a security bug. You can write scripts and small tools and contribute to an existing codebase with review.

    Recent findings suggest that you build with AI, not just chat with it. You use AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot or similar) in your daily work to write tools, analyse code or automate tasks. And you know their output still needs a second look, especially when it comes to security.

    Industry observers note that clear, friendly communication with engineers. You see yourself as an enabler, not a gatekeeper, and you can explain risk to people who aren't security specialists.

    Some Python and/or JavaScript experience, or experience building internal tools.

    Industry observers note that willingness to learn and use Camunda, since we build a lot of our own security automation on it. Prior BPMN / workflow experience is a plus.

    Experience responding to security incidents or being part of an on-call rotation.

    Exposure to security advisories, CVE disclosure or bug bounty programmes.

    Knowledge of AI/LLM security risks (OWASP Top 10 for LLMs / agentic apps, prompt injection, tool abuse).

    Experience securing Kubernetes or container-based workloads, or open-source / B2B software.
